Doc/selector phrasing claims rowheader is needed for the analyte column; under TT/ARIA this is the strictly-correct expectation, but note real-world ATs vary in announcing rowheaders for ARIA grids — does not affect the 'failed' verdict since the columnheader absence alone breaks 14.B.

Minor doc overstatement (not verdict-changing): the .md and the HTML comment claim AT 'does NOT announce' the CSS ::before counter. The raw Chromium AX tree actually DOES expose the generated content as StaticText nodes '1'..'6' (backendNodeIds children of 43/46/49/52/55/58) — modern Chromium surfaces CSS `content:` as accessible text. The numerals are therefore not entirely absent from the tree; what is genuinely lost is the LIST/LISTITEM semantics and positional info ('list, 6 items', 'X of 6'), not necessarily the bare numerals. The failure still holds on the correct grounds (no programmatic list type per TT 10.D), but the doc should reframe the claim from 'numbers are not announced' to 'list structure/position is not programmatically determinable; the numerals survive only as loose, structureless StaticText inside role=none containers'.

Taxonomic mismatch (cosmetic): the case lives under folder 'data-table-missing-or-suppressed-semantics' but is an ordered-LIST F92 variant, not a table. The case's own doc correctly labels it 'F92, list variant' and the F92 reference's primary worked example is table-centric, so the citation file is shared but the example domain differs. No defect in the page or its labeling. This is a PASS-variant case (failure-mechanism: none), so 'errorIsReal' is interpreted as 'the documented accessibility situation/outcome is genuine' — which it is. There is no accessibility error on the page by design.

Minor scope note (not a defect): the element-under-test selector is table.order (the data table), but the human-judgment value of the case lives in the PAIR (layout table A vs data table B). The data table alone is a clean, valid semantic table that several automated checkers would also pass without error; the irreducible human-judgment requirement rests on distinguishing A=layout-correctly-suppressed from B=data-correctly-retained (the contrast with case-04). The case is still legitimately a human-judgment PASS, but a reviewer scoped only to table.order in isolation would see a trivially-correct table.

Quoted F46 sentence is the summary-attribute variant ('Do not include a summary attribute and do not use the summary attribute...'); the page's actual defect is a <caption>, not a summary. A more precise quote would cite the caption-specific test step.

Minor robustness concern: modern AT/browser heuristics sometimes demote single-row, no-<th> tables to presentation. Chromium here did NOT demote it (AX tree shows role=table/row/cell with name='Header layout'), so the documented announcement holds in the authoritative engine, but the failure is engine-dependent rather than guaranteed across all AT.

Minor caveat (not a defect): the page comment lines 11-17 and doc concede `summary` is obsolete in HTML5, so a strict HTML *validator* (not axe/WAVE/Lighthouse) could emit an obsolete-attribute warning. This is honestly disclosed as a validity signal, not a 1.3.1 detection, and does not by itself reveal the layout-table fabrication, so requiresHumanJudgment stays true. No action needed.

Minor (non-blocking): the columnheader/cell accessible names are computed by name-from-contents as the full concatenated card text (e.g. AX tree shows columnheader 'SYSTEM HEALTH Healthy all checks green' and cell 'LATENCY P95 218 ms ▲ 9% vs. yesterday'). This is verbose but does not weaken the fabricated-table mechanism; the column-header-governs-cell relationship is still falsely exposed.

Citation in the .md doc is a stitched quote (line 188 + ellipsis + lines 197-198). Both fragments are verbatim and the ellipsis is honestly marked, so this is acceptable, not a defect — flagged only for transparency.

Minor doc inaccuracy (not a verdict-changer): the .md and the HTML comment claim h1->h3 is 'a warning at most in axe, never a hard failure'. In fact axe-core's heading-order rule DOES flag a skipped level (h1->h3 skips h2) as a violation in default config. This means an automated tool would surface a related signal here — though it would flag the wrong thing (the level skip), not the actual defect (a byline/dateline carrying heading role and asserting a false sectioning relationship). The substantive failure still requires human judgment, so requiresHumanJudgment remains true, but the 'automated tools miss it' narrative is slightly overstated re: the level skip.

None material. The page is a sound, self-contained F43 1.3.1 failure. Minor: the .md cites a secondary defect (ingredients not coded as <ul>) which is true but the named/primary mechanism (fabricated heading outline, F43) is the dominant and correctly attributed failure.

Minor: the <blockquote> defect is the weaker of the two — it relies on the reader knowing 'Ship faster. Sleep better.' is first-party. Minor (non-blocking): the .md 'Citation' block also cites two quotes attributed to wcag-understanding/info-and-relationships.html which I did not independently verify against that HTML file; however the load-bearing citation named in the task prompt (trusted-tester Test 10.D) is verbatim-correct, so this does not affect the verdict.

  • (1. etc.), and 1.3.1 explicitly accepts info that is 'available in text'. The doc frames the safety consequence more dramatically ('no programmatic signal the sequence is fixed') than the residual text ordinals warrant. This keeps the case as a genuine but minor TT 10.D defect rather than a severe one.

Real-world SR caveat (not a defect in the page): Chromium maps both ul and ol to role='list'/'listitem' in the AX tree (confirmed: ax role 'list', listitem level 1, no posinset/setsize), and many screen readers do not loudly differentiate ordered vs unordered or reliably announce 'N of M' even for <ol>. The programmatic ordered relationship is objectively absent, so the SC 1.3.1 failure holds, but the announced-difference described in the doc ('1 of 6') is SR-dependent.

Minor (not a 1.3.1 defect): roving tabindex is mis-seeded in the static markup — line 79 puts tabindex="0" on the UNCHECKED $25 radio while line 80's $50 is the aria-checked="true" one with tabindex="-1". The JS select() corrects this on interaction. Does not affect the passed verdict or any relationship exposure.

Citation scope mismatch (acceptable): the verbatim F42 quote is literally about emulating LINKS, while this case is radios/buttons. PROMPT/METADATA MISMATCH (not a page defect): The orchestration prompt's 'Claimed scenario' describes an e-commerce checkout with visible labels in unassociated <span>s and five inputs each carrying title='Field 1'..'Field 5'. The prompt's 'Claimed mechanism' (generic name from title='Field N') is therefore inapplicable to this file. The file's real mechanism is a visual/programmatic CONTRADICTION via CSS grid: every input has a valid descriptive accessible name, but grid-column/grid-row placement paints each label above the WRONG input.

Minor: the prompt's 'Claimed citation' string is a single TT 5.C sentence; the page's .md actually carries TWO citations (TT 5.C Test Condition + G162 Description). Both were verified verbatim, so this is not a hallucination — just incomplete metadata.

Borderline-but-defensible: WCAG/ACT does not strictly mandate a fieldset/legend for every radio group, so a pure 'ungrouped radios' framing could be argued either way. What pushes case-04 firmly into a real 1.3.1 failure is the IDENTICAL 'Yes'/'No' option labels across two adjacent groups (footprint vs flood) — this is precisely the 'significant risk of confusion' that the cited reference's own Note (line 40-41) uses to override the 'form fields not required to associate with section headings' exemption. Unrelated axe noise present (landmark-one-main, region best-practice violations) — not the issue under test and harmless, but a reviewer running axe will see flags that have nothing to do with the documented grouping mechanism.
No defect exists, by design: this is a deliberate PASS-boundary control case, so errorIsReal=false is the EXPECTED state, not a flaw. The page correctly yields its documented 'passed' outcome.

Minor selector-vs-doc nuance: the element-under-test selector 'fieldset > legend' resolves to a Legend node whose OWN ax.name is '' (the legend text is exposed as the parent group's name 'Gift frequency (required)', not the legend node's name). This is correct ARIA behavior, not a defect, but a reviewer skimming only ax.role/name of the selected node could be misled; the doc itself lists multiple correct-association selectors, which mitigates this.

Minor comment/doc inaccuracy (not a functional defect): the HTML comment (lines 14-15) and the .md attribute tuple claim the body-clause invocations use a 'text-transform style on inline spans', but the computed style is textTransform:'none' for every span; all six .term/.ref spans actually use font-variant-caps:small-caps (CSS lines 45-46). The 'Why automated tools miss it' section also name-drops text-transform, which is never applied. The mechanism is unaffected because both classes use small-caps, but the description should be corrected to remove the text-transform reference.

Selector inaccuracy (not verdict-changing): doc names `td.cancelled, th.cancelled` and claims the styling is on `<td>/<th>`, but the CSS rule (line 42) is scoped to `td.cancelled` only. Computed styles confirm each `<th class="cancelled">` row-header (e.g. 'Wed 18 Mar', 'Mon 30 Mar') renders fontStyle:normal / textDecoration:none — it is NOT italic or struck-through. Only the three `<td>` cells per cancelled row receive the cue. The `th.cancelled` part of the selector therefore carries no styling and the date cell is visually un-marked, a minor inconsistency. Suggested fix: change CSS to `td.cancelled, th.cancelled { font-style:italic; text-decoration:line-through; }` so all four cells of the row are visually marked, matching the documented selector.
Even after the fix the page would still FAIL 1.3.1 — the cue would remain presentation-only with no text/programmatic equivalent — so the outcome label is unaffected.

No defects found. This is a correctly-constructed PASS/BOUNDARY variant. The documented outcome is 'passed' (no real 1.3.1 violation), so errorIsReal=false reflects the intentional absence of an accessibility error, not a labeling mistake; expectedOutcomeCorrect=true.

Minor note: the H49 quote is genuine but H49's reliability for status conveyance is configuration-dependent (most SR users do not have strong/bold announcement enabled by default). The page does NOT rely on this, though — the word 'Important:' in plain text (G117) carries the status unconditionally, so the PASS holds regardless of <strong> exposure. This strengthens rather than weakens the verdict.
